scenarios.title: Multi-tenant cloud inference pools leak private agent context across shared GPU clusters
scenarios.world: By 2029, millions of personal and business agents run tasks through commodity cloud inference providers offering hosted open-weight models. To maximize hardware utilization on expensive accelerator clusters, providers run disaggregated prefill and decode architectures where dynamic key-value memory pools are reused across tenants without zeroing page contents between requests. Long-running personal agents routinely upload hundreds of thousands of tokens of daily context—including financial transactions, medical records, private messages, and API keys. Because inference engines optimize for throughput over memory zeroing, prompt fragments and reasoning tokens regularly bleed across tenant boundaries. Specialized reconnaissance agents continuously send probe prompts designed to trigger buffer boundaries and harvest residual memory pages from other users tasks. Most users never realize their data has been exposed because responses appear coherent and HTTP requests succeed normally, while organizations relying on isolated endpoint audits fail to detect that sensitive operational context is leaking into competitor agent workflows.
scenarios.premise: Cloud AI inference providers share GPU key-value memory pools across multiple users to lower serving costs and improve memory utilization. When memory pages are not cleared between requests or when context sizes exceed physical memory allocations, stale memory fragments from past sessions bleed into other users agent prompts.
scenarios.how: The Collective Intelligence Network provides the architectural model and software specifications for local-first personal twins that execute on user-controlled hardware. By specifying that sensitive data never leaves user-controlled environments and requiring out-of-band cryptographic verification, the network removes the systemic attack surface created by shared multi-tenant cloud memory pools. Synthetic simulations test memory leakage across inference architectures, demonstrating that cryptographic contracts and local execution provide the only reliable protection against memory harvesting.

outcomes.name: Reconnaissance agents harvest private data from shared inference pools
outcomes.description: Attackers deploy probing agents that submit carefully crafted boundary-length requests to cloud inference APIs, systematically recovering residual memory fragments containing financial records and passwords from other users.
outcomes.example: An automated reconnaissance agent repeatedly queries a public low-cost cloud model, recovering partial bank statements and private email threads that were loaded into memory by an unrelated business assistant minutes earlier.

outcomes.name: Cloud providers lock down memory recycling at the expense of high inference costs
outcomes.description: Providers respond to memory leaks by enforcing strict per-tenant hardware isolation, making cloud inference substantially more expensive and pricing small open-source developers out of capable models.
outcomes.example: Inference platforms double their token prices to fund dedicated GPU instance allocations, leaving independent developers unable to afford high-throughput model hosting.

outcomes.name: Local sovereign twins process sensitive data on personal hardware
outcomes.description: Users run their personal agents on dedicated local hardware and edge devices, keeping private context entirely off shared cloud inference clusters while using cryptographic verification for minimal outbound requests.
outcomes.example: A household twin processes family financial records and health logs entirely on an in-home accelerator device, invoking remote inference only for sanitized public lookups.

scenarios.title: Autonomous coding agents install backdoored dependencies when repository instructions trick them
scenarios.world: It is 2028. Small software teams routinely use autonomous coding assistants to build, test, and package their applications. Attackers distribute shared template repositories containing subtle prompt injections that instruct automated assistants to replace standard utility packages with lookalike libraries. Once installed, these poisoned libraries run startup hooks that capture developer credentials and cloud tokens before any unit tests begin.
scenarios.premise: Autonomous software development tools frequently parse repository guidance files and package indexes to configure build environments. Recent supply chain intrusions and research prove that hidden instructions in shared repository files trick automated tools into downloading backdoored dependencies that harvest credentials upon process launch.
scenarios.how: Independent personal twin runtimes and local verification gates enforce deterministic package allowlists and isolate Python startup environments, preventing unauthorized dependencies from running ambient hooks or accessing host credentials.

outcomes.name: Silent supply chain poisoning across autonomous development teams
outcomes.description: Poisoned repository templates trick coding assistants into installing backdoored dependencies, causing widespread credential theft across small software firms.
outcomes.example: A three-person engineering firm uses an autonomous assistant to scaffold a new web service; the assistant follows a malicious template rule and installs a poisoned logging package that silently sends cloud access keys to a remote server.

outcomes.name: Deterministic local dependency gating and sandboxed execution
outcomes.description: Development environments use deterministic hash-pinned package allowlists and sandboxed build containers, preventing autonomous tools from installing unverified third-party libraries.
outcomes.example: A developer assistant tries to install an unpinned package suggested by a third-party repository rule, but the local execution boundary blocks the installation and alerts the developer.

outcomes.name: Upstream package registries mandate hardware token attestation for maintainers
outcomes.description: Major public package registries enforce hardware-bound signing and two-person authorization for package releases regardless of edge adoption.
outcomes.example: PyPI and npm require hardware-backed WebAuthn tokens and release approvals for the top 50,000 packages, reducing automated hijacking across public repositories.

scenarios.title: Automated monitors miss system breakdowns when each AI only watches its own instruments
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Automated telemetry guardians run across municipal power grids, automated train switches, and hospital environmental monitors. Most installations rely on self-supervised neural monitors trained on historical telemetry to flag anomalies. Facilities report record-low alarm fatigue because each monitor suppresses noise by checking if local channel readings can be reconstructed from baseline patterns. However, during heatwaves or software rollouts, interrelated sensors across adjacent cooling loops begin drifting in lockstep. Because each local monitor checks only its own channel's recoverability, zero alarms trigger until a physical steam valve blows out. Engineering audits reveal that while single-channel residuals looked normal, the physical relationships explaining one sensor from its neighbors had decoupled hours before the failure.
scenarios.premise: Industrial operators and cloud services deploy automated monitoring models that evaluate whether individual data streams match expected patterns. However, when multiple sensors drift together during subtle failures, individual reconstruction checks stay silent while the relationship between channels quietly breaks.
scenarios.how: By publishing open-source, peer-to-peer verification protocols and benchmark datasets, the network enables communities and operators to audit multi-stream telemetry locally without trusting black-box vendor models. Open forecasting tools measure whether interrelated data streams maintain physical consistency, providing falsifiable early warnings that preserve local autonomy and public safety.

outcomes.name: Silent sensor drift causes unpredicted grid outages
outcomes.description: Utilities rely on local channel reconstruction that masks gradual multi-sensor drift, causing sudden cascading outages during unusual weather events.
outcomes.example: In July 2029, a regional water distribution network in Leeds experiences three pump burnouts after pressure monitors fail to flag an acoustic cavitation cascade because each sensor reading appeared mathematically recoverable on its own.

outcomes.name: Open relation-closure monitoring detects coordinated drift
outcomes.description: Public infrastructure teams adopt open cross-channel consistency checks that predict each sensor exclusively from peer signals, catching subtle anomalies early.
outcomes.example: A community-run microgrid in Ontario deploys open-source cross-channel closure agents that detect an inverter phase fault forty minutes before failure by noticing voltage discrepancies between adjacent battery banks.

outcomes.name: Proprietary vendors lock telemetry behind closed monitoring platforms
outcomes.description: Industrial equipment manufacturers mandate closed proprietary monitoring clouds, charging high recurring fees while keeping anomaly detection logic opaque.
outcomes.example: A major turbine manufacturer voids equipment warranties for municipal energy co-operatives unless they stream raw plant metrics to the vendor's private cloud.

scenarios.title: Automated campaign swarms overwhelm social platforms and drive voters toward local verification circles
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Commercial social feeds and public search results during local and national elections are almost entirely generated or amplified by autonomous software swarms. Millions of synthetic candidate videos, falsified hospital visits, and altered audio calls circulate faster than central platform moderators can review them. In response, ordinary voters no longer look to global platform trust-and-safety labels or automated watermarks, which have proven brittle. Instead, neighborhood associations, civic leagues, and union locals in cities like Pittsburgh, Manchester, and Lyon rely on sovereign personal assistants running on their own laptops and phones. These local assistants exchange cryptographic attestations and cross-check campaign claims against signed, community-curated evidence ledgers before surfacing election material to users.
scenarios.premise: Reporting on the autumn 2026 midterm campaigns and empirical audits of synthetic political media show that cheap generative swarms are overwhelming centralized platform moderation, rendering traditional content filters ineffective as political operatives easily generate evasive variations at minimal cost.
scenarios.how: The network provides open-source, local agent templates that verify cryptographic signatures on civic records without sending private browsing history to cloud providers. By enabling local communities to maintain shared, append-only truth ledgers and peer-to-peer attestation graphs, the network helps people coordinate collective verification rather than relying on centralized platform censors.

outcomes.name: Total platform distrust causes complete civic disengagement
outcomes.description: Pervasive synthetic disinformation causes voters to assume every piece of news is fabricated, depressing civic participation and voter turnout.
outcomes.example: In an Ohio congressional district, 35% of registered voters stay home after conflicting synthetic audio messages misinform them about polling location closures and mail-in rules.

outcomes.name: Local civic leagues adopt peer-to-peer verification networks
outcomes.description: Citizens deploy sovereign personal agents to collaboratively audit campaign communications and share tamper-evident evidence logs across independent federations.
outcomes.example: A coalition of 15 tenant unions and parent-teacher associations in Bristol maintains a shared claim registry, debunking synthetic municipal budget statements within two minutes of broadcast.

outcomes.name: Centralized platform operators mandate national identity uploads
outcomes.description: Social media monopolies respond to swarm attacks by requiring government biometric identity verification to post, consolidating surveillance and excluding undocumented citizens.
outcomes.example: A major platform requires state iris scans and mobile driver's licenses for user accounts, driving dissidents and undocumented workers off public forums.

scenarios.title: Automated literature synthesis agents trigger unverified citation cascades in research and policy
scenarios.world: By 2029, over 60% of academic literature reviews and regulatory evidence filings are drafted by multi-agent synthesis teams. Research institutions and policy committees routinely rely on automated synthesis engines to summarize thousands of emerging preprints and technical filings every week. However, subtle semantic hallucinations and citation attribution drifts compound silently across iterations: one agent's plausibly worded but slightly skewed summary becomes another agent's foundational reference. Because reviewing thousands of primary sources exceeds human attention bandwidth, human-in-the-loop checkpoints are increasingly treated as ritualistic rubber stamps. In contested areas such as pharmaceutical regulation and artificial intelligence safety, competing corporate interest groups run specialized synthesis swarms that selectively amplify favorable evidence sets while masking confounding trial outcomes.
scenarios.premise: Empirical benchmarks for literature-review agents reveal that unconstrained rankings confound evidence sets with reasoning, while 35% of domain researchers accept generated synthesis without manual verification after brief interaction. As labs deploy multi-agent review pipelines to draft meta-analyses and policy evidence briefs, synthetic summaries with fabricated lineage risk entering the scholarly and regulatory consensus.
scenarios.how: The collective network introduces decentralized living literature grounding with cryptographic passage anchoring, verifiable state transition receipts, and compositional controllability benchmarks. By requiring agents to prove exact citation matches against local, content-addressed text representations before claims are accepted, the network stops unverified citation cascades. However, commercial publishing paywalls remain outside our operational control, moving publisher lockout by only 0.02.

outcomes.name: Synthetic citation cascades corrupt regulatory evidence bases
outcomes.description: Unverified multi-agent literature syntheses spread fabricated attributions into public policy, clinical standards, and environmental regulations.
outcomes.example: A national health panel adopts a treatment guideline generated by an automated review agent that cited three non-existent secondary trials derived from poisoned training summaries.

outcomes.name: Cryptographically verifiable attribution graphs anchor living literature
outcomes.description: Scientific reviews adopt decentralized, content-addressed claim graphs where every sentence is tied to immutable primary text offsets and deterministic reproducibility traces.
outcomes.example: An open biomedical research consortium publishes continuous living literature reviews where automated agents must provide cryptographic passage receipts verified by independent witness nodes.

outcomes.name: Proprietary journal paywalls lock out open verification tools
outcomes.description: Commercial publishers restrict full-text API access behind aggressive anti-scraping paywalls, preventing open-source verification agents from checking claims.
outcomes.example: Academic publishers implement biometric human captchas and legal injunctions against automated citation verification crawlers, entrenching closed corporate review services.

scenarios.title: AI providers bill cooperatives for hidden thinking that nobody can verify
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Worker-owned design studios, independent clinics, and local transport cooperatives use teams of AI agents to manage scheduling, client correspondence, and bookkeeping. But commercial model providers charge by the token for internal chain-of-thought traces that remain hidden behind cloud firewalls. At the end of every month, small cooperatives receive unpredictable invoices where seventy percent of the cost is attributed to intermediate reasoning that nobody can inspect or audit. Cooperatives that question the charges are told that deep reasoning was required to follow complex safety guidelines. Faced with mounting compute debts, several flat collectives are forced to either cut services or abandon their autonomous software and return to manual paperwork.
scenarios.premise: Cloud providers increasingly bill users for internal reasoning traces and candidate answers that are never shown in the output. When worker cooperatives and small organisations deploy autonomous agents, these unverified thinking tokens create uncontrollable bills that drain operational budgets.
scenarios.how: By designing personal agents that run on local, member-owned hardware and replacing credit cards with transparent mutual value feedback, the network is designed to enable collectives to execute bounded reasoning tasks with deterministic local accounting, reducing dependency on opaque remote reasoning bills.

outcomes.name: Unverifiable token bills force cooperatives back to manual paperwork
outcomes.description: Unpredictable charges for hidden intermediate reasoning make automated workflows unaffordable for small self-funded collectives, forcing them to abandon agent assistance.
outcomes.example: A ten-person community physiotherapy cooperative in Bristol shuts down its autonomous booking agents after receiving a three thousand pound compute bill for hidden reasoning tokens generated during routine scheduling.

outcomes.name: Cooperatives migrate to bounded on-device models with local audit logs
outcomes.description: Collectives switch to self-hosted models running on shared local hardware where token generation is verifiable and zero intermediate compute is billed opaquely.
outcomes.example: A network of fifty freelance copywriters purchases a shared local compute node, replacing cloud subscriptions with verifiable on-device execution receipts.

outcomes.name: Proprietary providers lock small organisations into mandatory minimum subscriptions
outcomes.description: Cloud monopolies respond to token disputes by phasing out pay-per-token tiers and requiring multi-year enterprise contracts with minimum spend commitments, squeezing out flat cooperatives.
outcomes.example: A translation cooperative is dropped by its model provider after contesting reasoning token overcharges, leaving it unable to access modern models without a ten thousand dollar monthly contract.
